notes: Arbitration Act sections 43 and 44 application; Colman J's limits on non-party disclosure are clearly reasoned.

enrichment.short_title: Assimina Maritime: sections 43 and 44 and non-party evidence in Karachi grounding arbitration
key_facts: The tanker TASMAN SPIRIT grounded in Karachi port channel on a voyage from Kharg Island, causing massive pollution and a total loss claimed at over US$6.5 billion.
Shipowners alleged breach of the safe berth warranty and sought HR Wallingford feasibility study material held by Wallingford for Karachi Port Trust.
Wallingford declined disclosure at KPT's request; shipowners applied under sections 43 and 44 of the 1996 Act with tribunal permission.
Relief was framed as non-party disclosure under CPR 31.17, which Colman J held was unavailable under section 44.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commercial Court arbitration application for orders against a non-party witness/document holder in support of pending London arbitration.
enrichment.outcome: Orders granted under section 44 for inspection and copying of specifically described Wallingford documents sent to KPT and created in preparing them, plus a witness summons under section 43; shipowners ordered to pay Wallingford's compliance costs.
enrichment.ratio: Section 44 cannot be used for ordinary non-party disclosure under CPR 31.17, but may authorise preservation, inspection or copying of specifically identifiable documents where a question arises in the arbitration as to those documents; section 43 witness summonses require the same specificity and cannot be used as a discovery exercise.
legal_issues: Whether section 44 permits non-party disclosure equivalent to CPR 31.17
Whether Wallingford's channel study documents raised a question in the arbitration justifying section 44 orders
Whether a section 43 witness summons could compel production of broadly defined document classes
How narrowly the documents to be copied must be described
linked_authorities: BNP Paribas v Deloitte and Touche LLP [2001] 1 Lloyd's Rep 233

confidence.notes: Statutory construction and final order are set out expressly; grounding causation remains for the arbitration.

notes: Shared-care income-based JSA appeal; discrimination and remedy analysis is detailed though fact-specific.

enrichment.short_title: Hockenjos: child benefit link in income-based JSA and shared care sex discrimination
key_facts: Mr Hockenjos shared roughly equal residence of two daughters with his former wife under a joint residence order.
Income-based jobseeker's allowance child supplements were linked to receipt of child benefit, which in shared care cases usually went to the mother.
The father received no personal allowance or family premium for one daughter and challenged the scheme as indirect sex discrimination.
Commissioner Mesher held regulation 77's child benefit link was not objectively justified; the Secretary of State cross-appealed.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a Social Security Commissioner decision on entitlement to income-based jobseeker's allowance in a shared care case.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed and cross-appeal dismissed; JSA to be recalculated under paragraphs 93 and 94 of Scott Baker LJ's judgment and remitted to the Commissioners if not agreed.
enrichment.ratio: Linking JSA child supplements to receipt of child benefit indirectly discriminates against male shared carers in breach of Article 4 of Directive 79/7/EEC and cannot be objectively justified where other income-related benefits use a 'normally lives with' test; the Apportionment Act 1870 does not apply to weekly JSA awards.
legal_issues: Whether regulation 77 offended Article 4 of Directive 79/7/EEC
Whether the child benefit link was objectively justified
How shared care fathers should receive child premium and personal allowances
Whether the Apportionment Act 1870 applied to weekly JSA payments
linked_authorities: Jackson and Cresswell v Chief Adjudication Officer [1992] ECR I-4737

confidence.notes: Core discrimination holding and remedy order are clear; detailed calculation mechanics were remitted.

notes: Magazine cover copyright trial; copying findings and dismissal are comprehensive.

enrichment.short_title: IPC Media v Highbury: copyright in IDEAL HOME and HOME magazine covers
key_facts: IPC published IDEAL HOME, the market leader in home design magazines; Highbury published the rival monthly HOME.
IPC alleged that covers and internal sections of HOME issues from May to August 2002 copied copyright material from earlier IDEAL HOME issues.
Both publishers continually refined cover layout, typography, photography and masthead design from issue to issue.
Highbury denied copying and argued similarities were generic design choices or coincidence.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of a copyright infringement claim concerning magazine covers and selected internal articles.
enrichment.outcome: Claim dismissed; the court found no copying and held that even inspiration at a high level of generality would not amount to infringement.
enrichment.ratio: Copyright in original artistic works including magazine covers is infringed only by copying the work as a whole or a substantial part, not by adopting general layout ideas or industry-standard design features; selective comparison exaggerating similarities does not prove copying.
legal_issues: Whether Highbury copied IDEAL HOME covers or internal articles
Whether similarities resulted from common design techniques rather than copying
Whether partial mutilation of IPC copies in Highbury's disclosure indicated deliberate copying
Whether inspiration at a general level could infringe copyright

confidence.notes: Final finding of no copying and dismissal are explicit across covers and internal articles.

notes: Disability Discrimination Act airport wheelchair case; joint liability and contribution analysis is clear.

enrichment.short_title: Ross v Ryanair: wheelchair charges and airport access under the Disability Discrimination Act 1995
key_facts: Mr Ross, who had cerebral palsy and arthritis, was charged £18 on each occasion to hire a wheelchair at Stansted for Ryanair flights to Perpignan.
Ryanair provided free assistance only to passengers travelling with their own wheelchair; other disabled passengers were referred to a paid ground-handling agent.
Industry practice and aviation guidance treated airlines, not airport operators, as responsible for assistance from check-in to the gate.
The county court judge found Ryanair liable but acquitted Stansted Airport Ltd (STAL).
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal and cross-appeal from a county court judgment on unlawful disability discrimination in airport wheelchair provision.
enrichment.outcome: Ryanair's appeal dismissed in part; STAL also held to have unlawfully discriminated; STAL ordered to contribute 50% of Ryanair's damages and interest liability.
enrichment.ratio: Both an airline issuing a boarding card and an airport operator permitting airside access are providers of services under Part III of the 1995 Act; the transport exception does not apply to check-in to gate assistance; both must provide a free wheelchair as a reasonable alternative or auxiliary aid, and financial means of an individual disabled person is irrelevant.
legal_issues: Whether Ryanair's service was exempt as use of a means of transport
Whether STAL or Ryanair was the provider of airside access services
Whether charging for wheelchair hire was less favourable treatment under section 19(1)(d)
Whether STAL and Ryanair owed section 21 duties to provide a free wheelchair
linked_authorities: Roads v Central Trains Ltd [2004] EWCA Civ 1541

confidence.notes: Liability findings for both defendants and 50% contribution order are clearly stated.

notes: Section 33 discretion in historic abuse claim; appellate deference to first instance is central.

enrichment.short_title: T v Boys and Girls Welfare Service: section 33 discretion in historic care home abuse claim
key_facts: The claimant was sexually abused by a staff member at Tanllwyfan children's home in 1975-76 while in local authority care.
Proceedings were issued in June 2002, the first notice to the defendants, after the abuser's later conviction and a North Wales abuse inquiry.
The judge held date of knowledge was June 1997 but refused to disapply limitation under section 33.
Evidence cogency was weakened by lost records, uncorroborated abuse and psychiatric causation difficulties after 28 years.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from a preliminary hearing dismissing a historic abuse claim after refusal to exercise the section 33 discretion.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; the judge's refusal to disapply limitation was within his discretion and not open to appellate interference.
enrichment.ratio: Section 33 requires an equitable balance of prejudice; in stale historic abuse cases the longer the delay after accrual the harder it is to disapply limitation, and a fair trial may be impossible even where only two years elapsed after the extended limitation period; solicitor delay should not automatically be visited on the claimant but stale claims themselves prejudice defendants.
legal_issues: Whether the judge misdirected himself on the relevant delay under section 33(3)(a) and (b)
Whether a fair trial remained possible after 28 years
Whether solicitor delay should be attributed to the claimant under section 33(3)(e)
How Bryn Alyn principles apply to section 33 discretion in abuse claims
linked_authorities: CD v Bryn Alyn Community (Holdings) Ltd [2003] EWCA Civ 85

confidence.notes: Single issue appeal on discretion; judge's approach and dismissal are clearly recorded.

notes: Street robbery sentence appeal; exceptional circumstances jurisprudence is the focus.

enrichment.short_title: R v Cowell: exceptional circumstances and community sentence for group street robbery
key_facts: Richard Cowell, a university student of previous good character, was present throughout a midnight group robbery in Harrow involving eight or nine youths.
He played no active part but was convicted after retrial while a co-defendant was acquitted by the same jury.
The judge sentenced him to 12 months in a young offender institution, treating AG Ref Nos 4 and 7 of 2002 as requiring custody absent exceptional circumstances relating only to the offence.
A pre-sentence report recommended community punishment and assessed reoffending and public harm risk as low.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against sentence by leave of the single judge after conviction for robbery following retrial.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; 12 months' detention set aside and replaced with a 100-hour community punishment order, subject to the appellant's consent.
enrichment.ratio: Exceptional circumstances for avoiding custody after Attorney General's Reference Nos 4 and 7 of 2002 are not limited to circumstances relating only to the offence; they may include the real possibility that a meaningful community sentence would better protect the public than custody.
legal_issues: Whether AG Ref Nos 4 and 7 of 2002 required a custodial sentence
Whether exceptional circumstances are confined to offence-related factors
Whether the judge's preferred community approach was precluded by authority
Appropriate sentence for a foot-soldier present but inactive in group street robbery
index_terms: Attorney General's Reference Nos 4 and 7 of 2002
linked_authorities: Attorney General's Reference Nos 4 and 7 of 2002 [2002] 2 Cr App R (S) 77
Attorney General's Reference No 31 of 2003 [2004] EWCA Crim 1934
Attorney General's Reference No 37 of 2004 [2004] EWCA Crim 1854

confidence.notes: Sentencing error and substituted community order are clearly explained.

notes: Hotel fire insurance trial; policy construction and cleaning conditions are analysed in detail.

enrichment.short_title: Paine v Catlins: hotel kitchen fire and grease-cleaning warranty construction
key_facts: A fire starting on the kitchen range at the Shant Hotel spread via grease in the canopy plenum/extract duct and destroyed the hotel in September 2002.
Reinstatement and losses were claimed at about £2 million against insurers with a £1.6 million reserve.
Insurers argued breach of policy conditions requiring regular cleaning of extraction hoods and maintenance of the kitchen.
A major dispute concerned whether the horizontal canopy plenum counted as part of the hood subject to monthly cleaning.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Technology and Construction Court trial on insurers' defence that warranty conditions were breached, defeating indemnity for the fire loss.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; declaration that insurers were liable to indemnify Mr Paine under the policy because the alleged breaches were not made out.
enrichment.ratio: Policy conditions requiring extraction hoods to be cleaned as necessary must be construed commercially and cannot impose impossible cleaning obligations regardless of access; mere presence of grease residue in the canopy plenum does not without more prove breach of Conditions 3 or 4(ii)(B).
legal_issues: Whether the canopy plenum/extract duct fell within monthly hood cleaning obligations
Construction of 'cleaned as necessary' in the policy conditions
Whether grease accumulation alone proved breach of Conditions 3 and 4(ii)(B)
Consequences of any breach for indemnity

confidence.notes: Final declaration of insurer liability is explicit though quantum was not resolved.

notes: Fixed-term employee regulations appeal; pure point of law clearly resolved.

enrichment.short_title: DWP v Webley: fixed-term contract expiry and the 51-week Civil Service rule

statutes_considered.title: Fixed-Term Employees (Prevention of Less Favourable Treatment) Regulations 2002

key_facts: Mrs Webley worked at Leyton Jobcentre on successive Civil Service fixed-term contracts totalling about 51 weeks.
Her final contract ended on 17 January 2003 despite a continuing need for her services; other temporary staff were engaged.
She claimed less favourable treatment because permanent employees would not have been dismissed at 51 weeks under the Department's policy.
The Employment Tribunal chairman dismissed the claim on a preliminary issue; the EAT allowed appeal holding non-renewal could be less favourable treatment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to the Court of Appeal on a preliminary point of law whether non-renewal of a fixed-term contract alone can breach regulation 3.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; EAT decision set aside and Mrs Webley's tribunal application dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Fixed-term contracts are lawful and their termination by effluxion of time is an inherent feature, not of itself less favourable treatment or a detriment under regulation 3(1); the regulations prohibit differential treatment during the contract and abuse through successive fixed terms, not abolition of fixed-term employment.
legal_issues: Whether non-renewal after 51 weeks was less favourable treatment under regulation 3(1)(a) or (b)
Whether the 51-week Civil Service rule was objectively justifiable
Whether expiry of a fixed-term contract is necessarily a detriment
Proper formulation of preliminary issues in employment tribunal proceedings
linked_authorities: Whiffen v Milham Ford Girls School [2001] ICR 1023

confidence.notes: Pure legal issue on undisputed facts; Court of Appeal conclusion is unequivocal.

notes: Large design-right trial over vacuum cleaner spare parts; must fit/match analysis dominates.

enrichment.short_title: Dyson v Qualtex: unregistered design right in vacuum cleaner pattern spare parts
key_facts: Dyson sued Qualtex, a leading supplier of duplicate 'pattern' spare parts, for infringement of unregistered design right in numerous Dyson vacuum cleaner components.
Qualtex argued the must fit and must match exceptions excluded design right in most externally visible spare parts.
The 14-day trial involved over 20 witnesses and complex questions of originality, commonplace, surface decoration, waiver and acquiescence.
Parts in issue included wand handles, hose cuffs, brush bars, soleplates and tool adaptors across several Dyson models.
enrichment.procedural_posture: High Court trial of a design right infringement claim concerning aftermarket spare parts for Dyson vacuum cleaners.
enrichment.outcome: Claim succeeded; Qualtex infringed Dyson's unregistered design rights in the copied parts and acquiescence or estoppel did not bar relief.
enrichment.ratio: Design right can subsist in original parts of a larger article where must fit and must match exceptions are narrowly applied to features whose shape is dictated by interface requirements or design dependency on the whole product; subsidiary decorative ribbing may still be protected, and pattern parts copying non-excluded features infringe.
legal_issues: Scope of the must fit and must match exceptions in section 213(4) CDPA 1988
Whether design right subsisted in individual spare parts and part-features
Originality and commonplace defences
Whether Dyson acquiesced in Qualtex's pattern parts market
linked_authorities: Ford Motor Co Ltd v Reliant Motor Co Ltd
DKB Retail Ltd v Totes Isotoner (UK) Ltd [2004] RPC 16

confidence.notes: Overall infringement conclusion is clear though the judgment addresses many part-specific sub-issues.

notes: Put option construction appeal; registered proprietor requirement and reassignment issue resolved.

enrichment.short_title: BP Oil v Lloyds TSB: personal put option and registered proprietor requirement
key_facts: Lloyds granted BP group companies a personal put option to reassign a 25-year lease of Stoke Mandeville premises back to Lloyds for no consideration.
Mobil released its interest and the lease was assigned between BP entities, invalidating the first 2003 exercise notice.
The lease was reassigned back to all three option holders and a fresh notice was given in March 2004.
Lloyds argued the option was personal and could not be exercised after any intermediate assignment even on reassignment.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Cross-appeals from a trial on construction of a put option agreement ancillary to a lease assignment.
enrichment.outcome: Both appeals dismissed; all three purchasers had to be registered proprietors when giving notice, but temporary assignment did not permanently destroy exercisability once the lease was revested in them.
enrichment.ratio: A personal non-assignable put option requires strict compliance and must be exercised by all defined purchasers who are registered proprietors at the date of notice and not at the direction of a third party; clause 12 does not require continuous registered ownership throughout, so reassignment to the purchasers restores exercisability.
legal_issues: Whether the first exercise notice was invalid because not all purchasers held the registered lease
Whether the option ceased permanently on assignment to two BP companies only
Meaning of 'personal' in clause 12 beyond non-assignability
Application of break-clause authorities such as Max Factor and Equinox
linked_authorities: Max Factor Ltd v Wesleyan Assurance Society [1996] 2 EGLR 210
Equinox Industrial (GP2) Ltd v Sketchley Ltd [2003] EWHC 2 (Ch)

confidence.notes: Both construction issues and dismissal of cross-appeals are clearly reasoned.
